analysis.one_liner: Gives retail, food service, and cleaning workers the right to request schedule changes, with advance-notice and minimum-pay rules for their shifts.
analysis.headline: The bill, aimed at about 23.5 million low-wage workers in retail, food service, and cleaning jobs, was introduced in July 2014 and died in a Senate committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let any employee ask their employer for changes to hours, timing, location, advance notice, or stability of their schedule, and require the employer to discuss the request in good faith. For workers caring for a sick family member, in training, or working a second job, employers would have to grant the request unless they had a genuine business reason to deny it. For retail, food service, and cleaning workers specifically, it would require written schedules two weeks in advance, and pay when workers report for a shift that gets cut short, work a split shift, or have a schedule changed with less than a day's notice.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 23.5 million workers in retail sales, food preparation and service, and building cleaning — occupations with median pay between $9.15 and $10.44 an hour and where most workers learn their schedules a week or less in advance — would get predictable schedules, pay when shifts are cut short, and protection from retaliation for asking for changes. All employees would gain a right to request schedule changes for caregiving, health, education, or second-job reasons without fear of being fired for asking.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retail, food service, and cleaning workers

how_it_helps.text: Retail, food service, and cleaning employees would get their schedules in writing at least 14 days in advance, posted where they can see them, with one extra hour of pay for any shift changed with less than 24 hours' notice.

Workers sent home early would be paid for at least four hours, and workers required to call in to find out if they have a shift would get at least one hour of pay; split shifts would carry an extra hour of pay.

Every employee could request changes to hours, timing, location, notice, or stability of their schedule, and the employer would have to engage in a good-faith discussion and state the reason for any denial.

Requests tied to a serious health condition, caregiving, enrollment in a career-related education or training program, or a part-timer's second job would have to be granted unless the employer had a bona fide business reason to deny them.
The bill makes it unlawful to fire, demote, cut hours, or otherwise retaliate against workers for exercising these rights, with court enforcement, back pay, and attorney's fees for workers who win.

analysis.who_pays: Employers in retail, food service, and building cleaning would bear new labor costs — extra pay for short-notice changes, cut shifts, call-in shifts, and split shifts — plus the administrative cost of posting schedules two weeks ahead and running an interactive process for schedule requests. Businesses with 15 or more employees would be covered, and unionized workplaces with scheduling provisions in their contracts would be exempt.

drawbacks.text: Employers would face new labor costs and administrative burdens, including mandatory extra pay for split shifts, cut shifts, and schedules changed with less than 24 hours' notice, which small businesses and thin-margin restaurants would feel most.

The core right to request is weak for most workers: outside of caregiving, health, education, and second-job reasons, an employer may deny a request for any reason that is not unlawful, so the guarantee of schedule stability depends mainly on the notice and pay rules for three low-wage sectors.

The bill exempts employees covered by a collective bargaining agreement whose terms govern scheduling, so unionized workers would not get these protections if their contract handles schedules differently.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted real, documented problems — in the covered occupations, 66 percent of food service workers and 52 percent of retail workers learn their schedules a week or less in advance, and workers can be sent home unpaid when business is slow. The compliance costs fall on specific, low-margin industries, and honest supporters would acknowledge that extra pay mandates could lead some employers to schedule fewer hours or fewer workers. The design was narrower than its title suggests: the strongest guarantees apply only to retail, food service, and cleaning workers, while other employees get a process right that employers can sidestep with almost any lawful denial reason.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in July 2014 and referred to the Senate committee that handles labor law, and it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2015 without a hearing, a markup, or any vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Harkin introduced the Schedules That Work Act in the Senate on July 22, 2014, joined by Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Sherrod Brown.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where no further action was ever recorded.
Five Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill died in committee without reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Retail, food service, and building cleaning employers avoided the advance-notice, reporting-pay, and split-shift-pay mandates, while the low-wage workers the bill was written for gained nothing; the bill will have to be reintroduced from scratch in a later Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All six supporters — the sponsor and five cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican signed on; the bill received no floor action in either chamber.

industries.note: Would owe reporting-time pay, split-shift pay, and an extra hour of pay for short-notice schedule changes, and would have to post schedules 14 days ahead. In food service, 66 percent of workers learn their schedules a week or less in advance, so the costs would directly fund the predictability workers lose today.
Same scheduling, notice, and pay mandates would apply to retail employers with 15 or more workers, covering occupations where 52 percent of workers get a week or less of schedule notice.
Covered employers would face the same advance-notice and minimum-pay requirements for cleaners, janitors, and housekeepers.

industries.industry: Scheduling and workforce management software vendors
industries.note: The bill directs the Labor Department to run pilot programs using computerized scheduling software to create more predictable schedules, and compliance with 14-day notice rules would push more employers toward scheduling tools.
